raw.prompt: Without using any tools, write a detailed 700-word explanation of how terminal emulators work. No preamble.

raw.last_assistant_message:
A terminal emulator is a software application that simulates a physical terminal, providing a text-based interface for users to interact with a shell or command-line environment. To understand how they work, it's helpful to trace the journey of information from the moment you press a key until text appears on your screen.

At the core, a terminal emulator acts as a bridge between your keyboard and mouse on one end, and a shell process (like bash, zsh, or fish) running on your operating system on the other. When you launch a terminal emulator, it creates a new process on your computer and establishes a communication channel with a shell. This channel is bidirectional: it carries commands you type to the shell and returns output from the shell back to the terminal for display.

The input flow begins when you press a key. The terminal emulator captures this keystroke through its graphical user interface framework. Rather than sending the raw key directly to the shell, the terminal emulator converts it into a character or sequence of bytes that the shell can understand. For example, pressing the letter 'a' becomes the ASCII character 97. Special keys like arrow keys or function keys are translated into escape sequences—special multi-byte codes that convey meaning beyond simple characters. When you press the up arrow, the terminal emulator might send the sequence ESC[A, which the shell recognizes as a navigation command.

These keystrokes are written to a pseudo-terminal (PTY), a special device file that acts as a pipeline between the terminal emulator and the shell. The PTY has two sides: the master side, which the terminal emulator controls, and the slave side, which the shell uses. Think of it like a two-way pipe—data flows in both directions simultaneously.

The shell reads the input from its end of the PTY, interprets your commands, and generates output. This output—whether it's the results of a command you ran, error messages, or prompts—flows back through the PTY to the terminal emulator. The terminal emulator then processes this output and renders it visually.

Here's where terminal emulation becomes interesting: the shell often sends not just plain text but also control sequences that instruct the terminal emulator how to display that text. These sequences, part of the ANSI/VT100 escape sequence standard, tell the terminal to change text color, make text bold or italic, move the cursor to specific positions, clear portions of the screen, and much more. For instance, the sequence ESC[31m tells the terminal to display subsequent text in red color, while ESC[0m resets formatting back to normal.

The terminal emulator maintains a grid model of the display, typically tracking a matrix of characters with their associated attributes like foreground color, background color, and text styling. This is usually stored in a buffer, often called the terminal buffer or screen buffer. As the emulator receives output with escape sequences, it updates this buffer accordingly. When displaying the content, the emulator renders each character from the buffer using a monospace font, applying the appropriate colors and styles to each character based on the stored attributes.

Rendering happens continuously. When new content arrives through the PTY, the terminal emulator updates its buffer and refreshes the visible portion of the screen. Modern terminal emulators use GPU acceleration through graphics APIs to make this rendering smooth and efficient, though the fundamental process remains the same.

Another crucial aspect is handling the terminal size. Your terminal emulator window has dimensions—perhaps 80 columns wide and 24 rows tall, or larger if you've resized the window. When you resize the terminal emulator window, it notifies the shell of the new dimensions through a system call. The shell, in turn, adjusts its output formatting to fit the new constraints. Some programs respond to size changes by reflowing their output; others continue with the previous size until they're restarted.

Terminal emulators also manage scrollback buffers, allowing you to scroll up and review previous output. This scrollback history is typically stored in memory, separate from the active display buffer. The maximum scrollback size is configurable and represents a trade-off between memory usage and historical data retention.

Finally, terminal emulators handle various edge cases and special behaviors. They manage clipboard operations, allowing copy and paste functionality. They handle mouse events, which some terminal applications use for interaction. They also implement configuration options like color schemes, font selection, cursor style, and transparency.

The elegance of this system lies in its standardization. Because terminal emulators implement well-defined protocols and escape sequences, any shell or command-line application can run in any compliant terminal emulator. This universality is why you can use the same bash script on macOS in Terminal.app, on Linux in GNOME Terminal, or on Windows in Windows Terminal, and get essentially identical behavior.
